repos.title: CaPtain: A Pipeline for Post-Training Code-as-Policy Robot Agents
repos.paper_summary:
CaPtain is an open post-training pipeline that turns Qwen3.5-4B into a code-as-policy robot agent. The agent writes Python against 22 low-level perception, measurement, and guarded-motion primitives, with no grasp or place skills and no VLA at test time. Training has two stages: supervised fine-tuning on synthetic trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, then multi-turn RL with a privileged simulator critic that credits each request by its change in predicted success.

On held-out LIBERO (240 episodes), CaPtain-4B rises from 0% zero-shot to 55.4% after SFT and 73.8% after RL. On LIBERO-PRO it reaches 78.5%, above K1 (77.2%), WAA (75.6%), and ASPIRE (71.7%). RL gains of +17.6 to +21.2 points persist across three perturbation suites. Without target-domain training, it reaches 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX and 75.0 on CaP-Bench.

Limitations: RL trains only on the 40 LIBERO tasks with one 7-DoF arm. With 2 cm pose noise in the critic's state, its correlation with the privileged value drops to 0.49. Force-controlled tasks such as Wipe cannot be expressed with the current position primitives.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing robot code-writing agents rely on frontier models or pre-trained VLA skills, so small open models were never trained end to end.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work rarely trains the code-writing model itself, and end-to-end policies drop to 12.8% on LIBERO-PRO perturbations.

digest_headlines.heading: CaPtain
digest_headlines.headline: CaPtain pairs a 22-primitive harness with SFT on synthetic trajectories and RL using a privileged-state simulator critic.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: CaPtain-4B reaches 73.8% on held-out LIBERO after RL, up from 55.4% after SFT, and keeps its gains under perturbations.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Limits include RL trained only on LIBERO, critic accuracy that falls with pose noise, and no bimanual or force-controlled tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: CaPtain turns a 4B vision-language model into a standalone code-as-policy agent that deploys on a physical robot.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists implementation details, the robot API, RL settings, training infrastructure, and per-method comparison tables.

repos.title: CUA-Master: Scaling Computer-use Agents through Open-World Recursive Improvements
repos.paper_summary: CUA-Master is a training framework for computer-use agents built as two nested data-and-training loops. The outer loop feeds the model's observed weaknesses back into data collection and adds open-world material. The inner loop has two parts. Open-world seeding mines seed tasks and trajectories from instructional videos on YouTube, TikTok, and Bilibili, using transcript cues and frame-change triggers to locate actions. Autocatalytic propagation abstracts seeds into application-level primitives, composes them into single- or cross-application tasks with verifiers, and collects rollouts with snapshot-rollback retries. The agent uses GUI actions and shell CLI commands in one action space. CUA-Master-27B scores 80.2 on OSWorld Verified, 36.9 on OSWorld 2.0, 43.9 on WeaveBench, and 25.0 on Agents' Last Exam. The text provided contains no baseline numbers, and it ends before the training results, so the claimed gains over other models and across iterations cannot be checked here. The paper notes that video-derived trajectories may contain annotation noise and may not match real executions.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Computer-use agent training is limited by narrow, uncontrolled, and unreliable synthetic data, so the paper proposes a nested recursive framework.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: CUA-Master pairs an outer world-data-model flywheel with an inner data flywheel that mines tutorial videos and synthesizes verifiable tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: CUA-Master-27B scores 80.2, 36.9, 43.9 and 25.0 on four benchmarks, and mixing screen and shell actions beats screen-only execution.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The framework is reported to achieve competitive results and consistent gains across recursive iterations.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists related work, training data distribution, domain results, methodology prompts, action space, taxonomy, and limitations.

repos.title: Watch Your Step: Anticipated Perception for Humanoid Locomotion
repos.paper_summary: Watch Your Step introduces a perceptive locomotion framework for the Unitree G1 humanoid in which a lightweight foothold prediction model (FPM) predicts the next two footholds from proprioception and the velocity command, and the policy observes only small 7×7 elevation-map patches around those predicted footholds. The FPM is an MLP with two 128-unit hidden layers, trained by Huber regression on labeled footholds from recent policy rollouts and refit every 500 PPO iterations, jointly with a PPO locomotion policy. On the training terrain curriculum, the FPM policy reaches level 5 after 7.5k iterations, against 26.1k for the complete-map baseline (HM) and 20.0k for an attention-based encoder (AME2). AME2 ends slightly higher at 40k iterations but needs four GPUs and 6.3 s per policy update versus 0.55 s. In simulation, the FPM policy achieves 74.2% success on sparse corridor terrain versus 71.7% for AME2 and at most 42.7% for the other baselines, and 77.7% on out-of-distribution gaps. The policy transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 on stairs, a 0.55 m gap, and a 0.6 m drop. Limitations include reliance on an elevation map and that the policy's cautious behavior near unseen gaps is a hypothesis rather than a measured result.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Predicting footholds from proprioception and filtering the elevation map around them should cut redundant input for perceptive humanoid locomotion.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries
digest_headlines.headline: The locomotion task is set as a reinforcement learning problem for a 29-DoF Unitree G1 humanoid trained with PPO in 8192 parallel environments.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: A blind foothold predictor is retrained periodically, and the policy sees only small height patches around its two predicted footholds.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments and Results
digest_headlines.headline: The gated policy reaches curriculum level 5 in 7.5k iterations, 3.4 to 3.5 times faster than full-map methods.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: The approach trails full-map methods on stepped corridor terrain and cannot see obstacles approaching from the side.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Sampling the elevation map around predicted footholds learns faster than full-map policies and transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1.

repos.title: WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One Agent From Narration to Long-Form Video
repos.paper_summary: WeVisCut is a script-to-video system that pairs a stateful tool harness with a single 9B policy trained on executable editing traces. The harness tracks shared production state, validates tool calls, and returns typed blockers that the policy can act on. Editing inversion, verified replay, observe–reflect–repair, and trajectory materialization turn 3,750 finished Bilibili videos into 134,771 training examples. The Qwen3.5-9B policy is trained with LoRA SFT, runtime-verified rejection-sampled fine-tuning, Guided-OPD, and RCF-DAPO, which compares rewards only within matched roles and contexts. On a 100-task benchmark scored with five metrics over five runs, it improves its base model by 16.0 points in Overall Score and reaches comparable performance to Claude Opus 5 with nearly 33× fewer generated tokens per successful output minute. It also outperforms task-matched native editors, Crayotter and VideoAgent, under a shared tool environment. Stated limitations: broader template coverage and more reliable retrieval are needed, and Overall Score has no uncertainty estimate.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: WeVisCut couples a stateful script-to-video harness with executable data and one 9B policy for narrated long-form video.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work contrasts WeVisCut with tool-agent training, video editing agents, and evaluations that do not link scripts, traces, and renders.

digest_headlines.heading: WeVisCut Agent Framework
digest_headlines.headline: A shared policy chooses tools over a stateful runtime that validates calls, keeps artifacts, and repairs shots before delivery.

digest_headlines.heading: Data Construction
digest_headlines.headline: Four-stage pipeline recovers editing intent from finished videos and replays it to produce executable training examples.

digest_headlines.heading: Training WeVisCut
digest_headlines.headline: Three phases train the policy by imitation, recovery learning on policy-reached states, and decision optimization within matched roles.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On 100 held-out tasks, WeVisCut reaches 90.5 Overall Score, close to Claude Opus 5 at 89.9, with far fewer generated tokens.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The trained 9B policy improves all five metrics over its base model and approaches Claude Opus 5 at lower generation cost.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists admission rules for replayed training data, loss and intervention schedules, reward formulas, evaluation protocol, and a sample trace.

repos.title: $\nabla$Mimic: Ultra-Efficient Humanoid Control with Differentiable Simulation
repos.paper_summary: This paper presents ∇Mimic, a first-order method for humanoid motion tracking that trains on exact simulator gradients, and NablaEngine, a differentiable GPU simulator for the Unitree G1. ∇Mimic clips each sample's action gradient relative to the batch median and regresses the policy onto gradient-derived action targets, which bounds each update step in radians. NablaEngine runs MuJoCo's full contact dynamics with fused GPU kernels and computes the adjoint of a control step as one megakernel. Its gradients match float64 finite differences, and its adjoint is 11.5× faster than the MuJoCo Warp adjoint. On all 40 LAFAN1 clips with one policy on one GPU, ∇Mimic reaches a normalized return of 0.82 in 20 minutes, versus 1.2 h reported for the world-model method SuperMimic, and 0.874 in 1.8 h. SHAC halts on exploding gradients within 0.06 h on NablaEngine. Limitations: only the G1 on flat ground, simulation only, and only LAFAN1 tested. The clipping bias is not quantified, and the PPO and MuJoCo Warp runs use single seeds.

digest_headlines.heading: 1 Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Exact simulator gradients, with two obstacles removed, match the world-model score for humanoid tracking in minutes instead of hours.

digest_headlines.heading: 2 Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work uses zeroth-order PPO, short first-order windows, smoothed contacts or learned models, but not exact full-contact simulator gradients.

digest_headlines.heading: 3 Background
digest_headlines.headline: Tracking on the G1 is posed as a windowed return whose pathwise gradient depends on the dynamics' derivatives.

digest_headlines.heading: 4 Exact and surrogate gradients
digest_headlines.headline: Exact simulator gradients are unbounded in rare samples and costly, while world-model gradients are bounded but biased.

digest_headlines.heading: 5 $\nabla$Mimic
digest_headlines.headline: Per-sample clipping and multistep regression onto gradient-derived targets keep exact gradient updates bounded.

digest_headlines.heading: 6 NablaEngine
digest_headlines.headline: NablaEngine runs the full G1 contact dynamics and its adjoint in one megakernel, 11.5× faster than the MuJoCo Warp adjoint.

digest_headlines.heading: 7 Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: ∇Mimic reaches 0.82 in 20 min and 0.874 in 1.8 h, while PPO reaches 0.64 after 3 h and SHAC halts at 0.06 h.

digest_headlines.heading: 8 Limitations and future work
digest_headlines.headline: Results cover one robot on flat ground, in simulation on LAFAN1, with single-seed baselines and unquantified clipping bias.

digest_headlines.heading: 9 Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Cutting tracking training cost from hours to minutes could make larger motion corpora practical for humanoid foundation models.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists task and reward details, engine kernel and adjoint derivations, timing protocol, and extended ablation and cost tables.

repos.title: L3G-World: Real-Time Infinite World Generation with Latent 3D Gaussian Memory
repos.paper_summary: L3G-World is a real-time world-generation framework built on a Latent 3D Gaussian Memory (L3G): 3D Gaussians that each store a VAE latent feature and are updated as video is generated. The memory updater, L3G-Mem, spawns Gaussians only where the rendered memory has low opacity or high RGB error, and refines visible Gaussians with residual updates. The video diffusion transformer, L3G-Gen, conditions on the memory rendered in VAE latent space, avoiding decode-and-re-encode. L3G-Gen is trained with rectified flow and distilled to a few-step student with AnyFlow, reaching 9.02 FPS on one H100. Against the most efficient prior explicit 3D-memory baseline per metric, the paper reports 26.7–38.9× fewer 3D primitives, 3.0–3.2× faster memory reconstruction, and 349–359× higher VAE-space rendering throughput. Baselines include GEN3C, Lyra 2.0, Spatia, NeoVerse, Yume 1.5 and Matrix-Game 3.0; training uses DL3DV and RealEstate10K. The provided text ends before the quality tables, so the generation-quality claims are unverified here. Limitations: memory depends on Depth Anything 3 for metric depth, and speed gains are measured against one baseline per metric.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Interactive world models face a cost-consistency trade-off, and a compact latent Gaussian memory is proposed to address it.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Works
digest_headlines.headline: Prior explicit 3D memories either accumulate dense per-frame primitives or optimize too slowly for real-time generation.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: A memory updater spawns Gaussians in uncovered regions, refines existing ones, and renders VAE latent features directly into the generator.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On the first of two datasets, L3G-World reaches the highest loop-closure PSNR, 16.00, among the compared methods.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion presents compact latent 3D memory as a practical foundation for scalable interactive world models.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives flow-map and Gaussian preliminaries, training and retrieval details, online reconstruction results, and limitations.

repos.title: ReplaySSM: Cache SSM Inputs, Not State
repos.paper_summary: ReplaySSM represents the SSM state as a checkpoint and a buffer of recent inputs to separate output computation from state updates. By unrolling the recurrence, it computes outputs from the checkpoint and cached inputs without writing the full state on every step. The checkpoint is updated only when the buffer fills, reducing dominant state memory traffic by roughly half. This design enables cheap speculative rollback via pointer moves and allows low-precision checkpoints for outputs while keeping high-precision checkpoints for recurrent updates, preventing quantization error accumulation. Implemented in vLLM for Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet, ReplaySSM accelerates standard decoding by 1.20–1.47× over tuned vLLM at batch size 256 across four hybrid models. It achieves about 1.8× the throughput of vLLM’s speculative decoding on two 120B-class models. Separating state precisions reduces output KL divergence by up to 36× compared to shared low-precision checkpoints. Limitations include that every step still reads the checkpoint, and the method requires managing circular buffers with capacity dependent on verification length.

repos.title: WorldCast: World-Consistent Character Video Generation with Large-Angle Camera Control
repos.paper_summary: WorldCast is a framework for character video generation under large-angle camera trajectories, released with CLACT, a dataset of 80,000 training samples (50,000 Unreal Engine 5 camera-motion sequences and 30,000 Blender samples with multi-view character anchors). Built on Wan2.1-I2V-14B, it back-projects the initial frame into a depth-based point cloud, scales camera translation to match a reference video, and renders the cloud along the target trajectory to provide geometric guidance and coverage masks. Geometry-Aligned Memory Attention (GAMA) estimates poses for the initial frame and character anchors with a multi-view geometry model, aligns them to the target trajectory with a Umeyama similarity transform, and injects view-relevant anchor features into video tokens through 20 zero-initialized blocks. Training has two stages: camera control on 76,698 SpatialVID sequences plus UE5 data, then GAMA on the Blender samples, updating only the memory bank and anchor adapter. The excerpt ends before the results section, so it reports no ATE, MEt3R, or image-quality values. The paper lists more flexible anchor acquisition, dynamic scenes, and longer or interactive trajectories as future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Large-angle camera motion couples trajectory accuracy with unseen character regions, so the paper introduces CLACT and WorldCast.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work covers camera-conditioned video, geometry-aware view synthesis, and identity-preserving generation, but not multi-view character anchors.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: WorldCast conditions a video diffusion backbone on projected geometric guidance and multi-view character memory through Geometry-Aligned Memory Attention.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On 42 scenes, WorldCast reaches the lowest absolute trajectory error of 0.065 among compared methods.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Ablations attribute gains to large-angle training data, camera-ray conditioning, anchor alignment and multi-view memory, while dynamic scenes remain future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers scale calibration, data construction, metric protocols and extra analyses, after ethics and reproducibility statements.

repos.title: ReLift: Dense 3D Tracking as Lifted Trajectory Repair
repos.paper_summary: ReLift is a feed-forward method for dense monocular 3D point tracking that repairs and completes trajectories lifted from pretrained 2D trackers and depth and camera models. Each 2D track is lifted along its viewing ray using the estimated range, and occluded observations are masked and filled by linear interpolation. A corrector alternates attention along each track with attention across tracks within each temporal chunk, and predicts per-frame XYZ residuals that are added to the lift. It trains only on clean PointOdyssey trajectories with randomized corruptions of ray direction, range, drift, and occlusion dropouts, so no tracker, depth model, or renderer runs during training. The same weights, without retraining, improve all six tracker–geometry pairings tested. On WorldTrack, ReLift reports the highest mean APD3D, improving on the strongest baselines by 2.1 on all points and 3.0 on dynamic points. Its faster configurations run 2.7–4.4× faster than 4RC. Limitations: accuracy remains sensitive to input geometry, and the simulated errors omit camera-pose errors and persistent identity switches.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Monocular dense 3D tracking can focus learning on repair and completion because pretrained 2D trackers and geometry models already handle correspondence and depth.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior methods fit 3D tracks with per-scene optimization or learn them feed-forward, while ReLift reuses 2D tracks and frozen geometry.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: A trajectory corrector alternates temporal and across-track attention to predict 3D residuals on lifted trajectories.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On WorldTrack, the corrector with CoWTracker and 4RC geometry reaches 89.01 mean all-point accuracy, above 4RC's 86.94.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Performance still depends on input geometry, and handling persistent correspondence errors is left to future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists preprocessing, architecture, training corruptions, evaluation protocol, baseline configurations and runtime measurements.

repos.title: ODE Policy: Robot Learning via Action Dynamics, Not Actions
repos.paper_summary: ODE policy learns the dynamics of a robot action, modeling the policy as a neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) whose vector field is conditioned on the observation. Each action is integrated from the previous one at inference, so the executed trajectory is continuous by construction. In imitation learning, the field is trained by matching integrated action chunks to demonstrations, and a contractive perturbation of chunk start points pulls states back toward the demonstrations. An optional diversity head supports multi-modal behavior. On LIBERO, it reaches 79.2% success after one epoch, against at most 43.2% for baselines. As the action head of π0.5, it reaches 96.0% against 75.5% for flow matching. It generates a chunk 10.8 times faster than flow matching in simulation. It has the highest success rate on all 14 real-world tasks. As the actor of SuperMimic in RL, it ends training with a return of 0.885 against 0.845. Limitations: encoding the binary gripper command as a field state lowers LIBERO success after one epoch from 79.2% to 74.5%. Early model-free RL experiments showed little gain and sometimes a loss. Several analyses use a single seed.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Most robot policies map observations to discrete actions and leave continuity to be learned; ODE policy instead learns the action's dynamics.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior ODE robot policies fix the vector field's form, and efficiency methods keep direct-action actors, which ODE policy changes.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries
digest_headlines.headline: Direct-action policies output each action separately, while a neural ODE defines a field integrated over time.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: The method integrates a learned action field over each chunk, trains it on integrated paths, and adds a sampled diversity offset.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: The evaluation compares ODE policy with 14 baselines on simulated and real tasks, with shared backbones, data, and training schedules.

digest_headlines.heading: Simulation Results
digest_headlines.headline: In simulation, ODE policy learns faster, needs fewer demonstrations, generates actions faster, and keeps multiple behavior modes.

digest_headlines.heading: Real-World Results
digest_headlines.headline: On four real robots, ODE policy has the highest success rate on each reported task and transfers dexterous skills across labs.

digest_headlines.heading: Ablation Studies
digest_headlines.headline: Ablations show that chunking is essential and that removing the contractive perturbation drops the one-epoch success rate from 79.8% to 58.4%.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Future Directions
digest_headlines.headline: Discussion argues continuity built into the policy improves efficiency across scales and suggests three preliminary extensions.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists benchmark and robot details, training settings, timing tables, and extra generalization, multi-modal, and ablation results.
